en: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung will attend summits of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) next week, his national security adviser said Thursday. The South Korean president will depart Monday first for Manila where he will attend the ASEAN summit until Tuesday, followed by a two-day trip to China's Shenzhen beginning Wednesday, where he will attend the APEC summit, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac told a briefing. On Monday, Lee plans to hold discussions with ASEAN countries on ways to enhance cooperation during a South Korea-ASEAN summit, followed by a meeting with leaders of five Mekong countries — Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar, Thailand and Vietnam. During the summit with the Mekong countries, the South Korean president plans to express his commitment to strengthening strategic partnership with the countries and discuss ways to enhance cooperation in critical minerals, responses to transnational crimes and others, Wi said. The following day, Lee will attend the ASEAN Plus Three summit, which will bring together the heads of state of ASEAN member countries, as well as South Korea, Japan and China, and later the East Asia Summit to discuss regional issues. Arriving in Shenzhen on Wednesday, the South Korean president will attend an APEC CEO summit, followed by a welcoming dinner hosted by Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan. The following day, he will attend the APEC summit and take part in discussions under this year's theme, "Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together," before returning home the same day. In his remarks at the summit, Lee will stress South Korea's pledge to play a constructive role in developing APEC and promoting the prosperity of the Asia-Pacific region, the national security adviser noted. At the upcoming summits, Lee also plans to strengthen mutual trust and cooperation with other heads of state through bilateral and multilateral meetings while highlighting South Korea's contributions to resolving regional challenges, including energy supply chains, transnational crimes and food security, according to Wi. The president also plans to call on ASEAN and APEC member countries to support Seoul's peaceful coexistence policy toward North Korea and convey a "positive message" in favor of peace and security on the Korean Peninsula, the official noted. A presidential official separately said that North Korea is unlikely to attend next week's APEC summit to hold talks with the United States. "It would be difficult to say there is zero possibility of talks (between North Korea and the U.S.), but I think the probability might not be high," the official said on condition of anonymity. The North is, in particular, unlikely to attend next week's APEC summit, the official said, adding that the chances of talks between the two sides during the summit are slim

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum is preparing for one of its most closely watched gatherings, with US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin expected to attend the leaders’ summit in Shenzhen, China. The meeting comes as geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and conflicts affecting global energy markets place growing pressure on international economic cooperation. The 21-member forum brings together economies responsible for a substantial share of global output and trade. Although APEC does not operate as a formal political or security alliance, its annual leaders’ meeting provides an important platform for major powers to discuss economic relations, investment, supply chains and regional stability. Here are five key facts about APEC and the issues likely to shape this year’s summit. Founded in 1989 in Canberra, Australia, APEC began as an informal dialogue involving 12 economies. It has since developed into the Asia-Pacific region’s leading economic cooperation forum, promoting trade, investment, economic growth and regional integration. The grouping’s 21 members account for approximately 62% of global GDP and around half of international trade, making it an important platform for discussions about the global economy. One distinctive feature is that APEC refers to its participants as “member economies” rather than countries. This arrangement allows both Hong Kong, which is governed by China, and Taiwan, which Beijing claims as part of its territory, to participate under their respective designations. However, India, despite being the world’s most populous country, is not a member. APEC also operates differently from organisations that impose legally binding obligations on their members. Its decisions are reached through consensus, and commitments are voluntary and non-binding. This allows economies with different political systems and strategic interests to participate without accepting a common set of enforceable economic rules. China is hosting APEC for the third time, following previous summits in Shanghai in 2001 and Beijing in 2014. This year’s choice of Shenzhen carries both economic and strategic significance. Located close to Hong Kong, Shenzhen is part of China’s Greater Bay Area, which also includes Macau. Beijing aims to develop the region into a major international centre for technology, finance and innovation. The city is also home to some of China’s most prominent technology and manufacturing companies, including BYD, Huawei and Tencent. Its economic transformation from a relatively small settlement into a major technology and industrial centre makes it an important showcase for China’s development model. Chim Lee, a senior analyst at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said the choice reflects both domestic and international considerations. Shenzhen provides China with an opportunity to highlight its technological capabilities, trade ambitions and resilience amid geopolitical uncertainty. Hosting the summit in the city also allows Beijing to present its vision of the Greater Bay Area as an increasingly important centre of global economic activity. The presence of several major world leaders is expected to make this year’s meeting particularly significant. Chinese President Xi Jinping is set to chair the leaders’ meeting and deliver remarks. US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are also among the expected participants, creating the possibility of high-level discussions involving three major powers. Other expected attendees include Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and the leaders of Canada, Australia, Mexico, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea and Vietnam. Taiwan has designated Stan Shih, founder of Acer, as its representative. Japan has not formally confirmed whether Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will attend, while New Zealand has yet to officially announce its delegation. The potential participation of Trump, Xi and Putin will attract particular attention because their countries have overlapping economic interests but sharply different positions on trade, security and international conflicts. However, the presence of leaders at the same summit does not necessarily mean that formal bilateral or trilateral agreements will follow. Several geopolitical and economic disputes are expected to shape discussions in Shenzhen. The economic consequences of conflict in the Middle East are likely to feature prominently. Disruptions to energy supplies and shipping routes can affect global trade, supply chains and inflation, creating challenges for economies that depend heavily on imported energy. For APEC members, the issue is particularly important because economic growth across the region remains closely connected to international trade and reliable energy supplies. The possible presence of all three leaders places their diplomatic interactions among the summit’s main points of interest. China has shown reluctance to participate in nuclear disarmament discussions, partly because its nuclear arsenal is smaller than those of the United States and Russia. Washington and Moscow may also seek to discuss the war in Ukraine, although their respective positions on China could differ. The summit could therefore provide opportunities for diplomatic contact, even if the leaders do not reach substantive agreements. Relations between Washington and Beijing will be another major focus. Both sides are facing difficulties in meeting commitments associated with an extended trade truce, according to analysts. Rare earth supplies, artificial intelligence, tariffs and technology restrictions are likely to remain important areas of disagreement. US arms sales to Taiwan will also be closely watched, given Beijing’s strong opposition to military cooperation between Washington and Taipei. These issues extend beyond bilateral trade. They affect global manufacturing, technology supply chains and the ability of businesses to operate across major markets. Regional security tensions will also influence the summit’s diplomatic environment. Relations between China and Japan have remained strained since November 2025, when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested that Japan could deploy its military if Chinese action against Taiwan also threatened Japanese territory. Beijing strongly objected to her remarks. China’s relationship with the Philippines is also under pressure because of continuing disputes in the South China Sea. These tensions involve maritime claims and competing interests over access to strategically important waters. The participation of both countries’ leaders could provide an opportunity for diplomatic engagement, although the underlying disputes remain unresolved. APEC consists of 21 member economies spanning the Asia-Pacific region: The diversity of its membership is one of APEC’s defining characteristics. It brings together advanced industrial economies, emerging markets and developing economies, allowing discussions on trade and investment across a broad geographical and economic landscape. The APEC leaders’ meeting is scheduled for November 18 and 19, preceded by an annual CEO summit on November 17 and 18. The discussions will take place against a backdrop of trade uncertainty, geopolitical competition and concerns about the resilience of international supply chains. The gathering’s significance will depend not only on the declarations issued by its members but also on whether major economies can maintain dialogue despite their differences. For China, hosting the summit offers an opportunity to demonstrate its economic influence and present Shenzhen as a centre of technological development. For the United States, Russia and other participants, the meeting provides a platform to engage with key regional economies while navigating competing strategic priorities. APEC’s consensus-based and non-binding structure limits its ability to resolve major geopolitical disputes. Nevertheless, its economic reach makes it an important venue for maintaining communication among powers whose decisions have consequences well beyond the Asia-Pacific region. Korean Peninsula issues may be sidelined as other crises take priority: analysts A summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un appears unlikely at next week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) gathering in Shenzhen, China, a Cheong Wa Dae official and security analysts said Thursday, despite Trump’s earlier talk of a potential meeting. The assessment comes as the Republican Party’s sweeping losses in the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections have weakened Trump’s momentum for unconventional diplomatic initiatives such as a meeting with Kim. Pressing international issues are also expected to dominate any talks involving the U.S. on the sidelines of APEC, including a possible one-on-one meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and three-way talks that would also involve Russian President Vladimir Putin. “We see little possibility of North Korea participating in multilateral events on occasions such as APEC, and little possibility of U.S.-North Korea contact taking place on that occasion,” the Cheong Wa Dae official said during a press briefing. Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies, voiced a similar view, ruling out a formal summit while leaving open a slim chance of a brief encounter. “The possibility of a summit around APEC period is zero,” Yang said. “As for an encounter, chances are not high either, but even a 1 percent possibility is still a possibility, so preparations are necessary.” Kwak Jin-o, a research professor at Pai Chai University, said a trip to China by the North Korean leader for a possible meeting with Trump would require preparations well in advance, suggesting it is already too late to arrange the summit. “For Kim Jong-un to make a move, preparations should already have been made,” he said. Moon Chung-in, a professor emeritus at Yonsei University, also pointed to the absence of groundwork, along with Pyongyang’s lingering distrust following the collapse of the 2019 Hanoi summit. “For a summit to take place, Washington would need to appoint a special envoy, establish preliminary contacts, set an agenda and form a task force to support the negotiations,” Moon said. “None of these preparations appear to be underway.” Moon dismissed speculation that Kim might agree to a spontaneous meeting, arguing that the North Korean leader would demand concrete incentives in exchange for curbing nuclear activities. “Kim will not come out just for a showcase. He still has the trauma of Hanoi,” he said. Bureaucratic considerations within North Korea's foreign ministry are another reason Moon sees little possibility of such a meeting. “Former Foreign Minister Ri Yong-ho was reportedly purged following the Hanoi summit’s collapse. Even though Foreign Minister Choe Son-hui wields considerable power, she would be reluctant to take such a risk without assurances of a successful outcome,” Moon said. The prospect of a Trump-Kim meeting drew attention after The Wall Street Journal reported on Aug. 18 that Trump was seeking talks with Kim, potentially during his November trip to China. Trump said the next day that he expected to meet Kim before the year’s end. Expectations faded on Oct. 19, however, when Trump said “I don’t know” about a possible meeting in China, with the Republic Party’s Nov. 3 midterms defeat further dimming hopes. Questions remain over how much attention issues on the Korean Peninsula will receive during the APEC gathering. The Cheong Wa Dae official said Seoul is closely following reports of a possible U.S.-China-Russia summit and communicating with relevant countries. “We cannot rule out the possibility of issues concerning the Korean Peninsula being discussed, so we are closely following the situation and maintaining the necessary communication with relevant countries,” he said. Analysts, however, were skeptical that the peninsula would feature prominently, given competing priorities such as nuclear arms control and the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine. “I do not see much possibility of issues concerning the Korean Peninsula being discussed in depth, although I would not rule out a passing reference to peace and stability on the peninsula,” Yang said. Moon also said Trump’s likely focus on resolving the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran could overshadow North Korea, further reducing Pyongyang’s willingness to engage. Kwak similarly expected any discussions to remain broad, potentially limited to denuclearization, and doubted Seoul would play a central role given Pyongyang’s opposition to its involvement. “South Korea’s role is important, but bringing South Korea into the discussion would draw objections from North Korea,” he said. Korea Times reporter Kim Bo-kyoung contributed to this article
